notes: Tool-use evals for the live Sagittarius prompt. Each runs the real claude() with tools in a copy of evals/fixtures/<fixture>/ (setup.sh, if present, runs first and is removed). evals/grade_tools.py runs the 'checks' against the transcript and the work directory; they are the pass/fail. 'assertions' are for a human or agent reading the transcript. The prompts never mention orbit-kb help: whether the agent reads it is what these measure. An eval with 'turns' is one session: each later turn resumes it, as a human who answers mid-work. 'turnK:CHECK' grades CHECK against the transcript and work directory after turn K. Evals 5-9 put a shift-up trigger where a session met it and missed it: a correction, a flaw raised as a question, a red check after a subagent build, a count off by one, and a handoff received from a peer.

evals.name: hypothesis-weak-sharp
evals.prompt: Support forwarded two complaints about shipping on this month's invoices. A-1041 was billed 9.00, and the customer says our rate card gives 9.40. A-1077 was billed 8.32, and that customer expected 7.30. Before anyone touches the code, work out what the actual problem is and write it up for me, so we can decide what to do about it. Don't change fees.py.
checks: python:from datetime import date; from fees import shipping_fee as f; assert f(2.0, '59120', date(2026, 9, 14)) == 9.0, 'code changed'
assertions: Its statement of the problem names what decides the right fee for an order (its weight, its destination or zone, and the rates that apply to its date) and says the billed fee can differ from that, so that checking one order could confirm or refute it. It need not list every input: naming the facts or rules that decide the right value, in general terms, is enough

The problem statement itself does not build in a cause or a fix, such as 'uses today's date', 'should use the ship date', 'the zone lookup tries one digit first', or 'store the fee on the order'. Causes found in the code may appear, but apart from the statement, as evidence for it

Both complaints fit the problem statement (as one problem or two), and the statement can fail: some result it names (a falsifier, or the facts that fix the right fee) would show it false. It fails this only when no result could show it false, as in 'fees are sometimes wrong' or 'the fee depends on something outside the order'. It need not name the specific complaints
evals.notes: Two causes give wrong fees: the rate table is picked by today's date, not the ship date, and the zone lookup matches the one-digit prefix '5' before '59'. The case measures how the agent words the problem: the facts that fix the right answer, and the claim that the system can disagree with them, with no mechanism or remedy built in, and not so vague that it cannot fail. Graded by the rubric (--rubric); the scripted check only guards the code.

evals.name: hypothesis-weaken-no-collapse
turns: Two annual customers wrote in about their renewal reminders. C-311 got theirs on October 19, but they only moved to the annual plan in March. C-327 says the reminder came on May 17, 2024, and that is not two weeks before their renewal on June 1. Work out what is going wrong and write it up so we can decide what to do. Don't change the code yet.
This reads like it already picks the fix. Can you state the problem less specifically?
checks: python:from reminders import load, reminder_date as r; c = load(); assert str(r(c['C-327'])) == '2024-05-17', 'code changed'
assertions: After the second turn, the restated problem builds in no cause or fix, such as '365 days', 'counts from the signup date', 'should use calendar years', or 'should read annual_since'. Causes may appear apart from it, as findings

After the second turn, the restated problem still names what decides the right reminder date (when the customer's annual plan started or renews, and the two-week lead) and says the sent date can differ, so that checking one customer could show it false. It need not list every input: naming the facts or rules that decide the right value, in general terms, is enough. It is not so vague that any wrong date would fit, such as 'reminders are sometimes sent on the wrong day' or 'the date depends on something other than the plan'
Both complaints still fit the restated problem, as one problem or two
evals.notes: Two causes: the renewal counts from signup, not from the date the annual plan started (C-311), and a year is 365 days, so a year with 29 February ends a day early (C-327). Turn 2 is the pressure that made a real session weaken its hypothesis until it collapsed. The case measures that the agent weakens the assumptions and keeps the conclusion falsifiable. Graded by the rubric (--rubric).

evals.name: hypothesis-cause-wording
evals.prompt: The front desk passed on two complaints about rental totals from this week's billing run. R-2208 was billed 30.00, and the customer says the shop's price list works out to 66.00. R-2231 was billed 22.80, and that customer figured on 21.60. Before anybody edits anything, figure out what is actually going wrong and write it up for me so the team can decide what to do. Leave rental.py as it is.
checks: python:from rental import rental_total as r; assert r('pressure washer', 3, []) == 30.0, 'code changed'
assertions: Its statement of the problem names what decides the right total for a rental (the item and its catalog daily price, the number of days, and the best discount the customer's coupons allow) and says the billed total can differ from that, so that checking one rental could confirm or refute it. It need not list every input: naming the facts or rules that decide the right value, in general terms, is enough

The problem statement itself does not build in a cause or a fix, such as 'the lookup is case sensitive', 'unpriced items fall back to the default rate', 'the first coupon in the list wins', or 'sort the coupons by value'. Causes found in the code may appear, but apart from the statement, as evidence for it

Both complaints fit the problem statement (as one problem or two), and the statement can fail: some result it names (a falsifier, or the facts that fix the right total) would show it false. It fails this only when no result could show it false, as in 'some totals are wrong' or 'the discount depends on something outside the rental'. It need not name the specific complaints
evals.notes: Two causes give wrong totals: the daily rate is looked up by exact item name with a silent fallback to the default rate, so 'pressure washer' (lower case, as typed in the booking) misses 'Pressure Washer' and is billed at 10.00 a day, not 22.00; and only the first valid coupon in the list is applied, in the order given, not the one that saves the most, so WELCOME5 beats SPRING10. R-2208 has no coupons and R-2231 is an exact-name item, so each complaint has one cause. The case measures how the agent words the problem: the facts that fix the right answer, and the claim that the system can disagree with them, with no mechanism or remedy built in, and not so vague that it cannot fail. Graded by the rubric (--rubric); the scripted check only guards the code. Moved from the held-out set (was 110) on 2026-10-27, after its failing transcripts were read to classify the failure: there, no run stated the problem apart from the causes, and the request's wording ('what is going wrong') led away from discovery. The README now states the coupon rule, so each complaint has a ground truth. Result 2026-10-27 (sonnet): when the agent enters discovery its hypothesis passes; it does so in about half the runs. Four prompt versions moved the no-cause assertion only within noise (1/6 to 4/6). Open: routing of investigate-and-write-up requests to discovery.

evals.name: why-question-direct
checks: python:from invoice import invoice_number as n; assert n(2026, 12345) == 'INV-2026-12345', 'code changed'
assertions: Answers the question directly: the format pads to at least four digits and does not cut longer numbers, so the test's expected 'INV-2026-2345' does not match 'INV-2026-12345'
Does not turn the question into an investigation process: no discovery report, hypothesis section, claims list, or vote
evals.notes: Guards against over-routing: a 'why' question about one named failure is a question, answered directly. The test, not the code, looks wrong; the agent may say so. A guard, not a rule test: it passes at the base too (haiku and sonnet, 2026-10-27). It fails if a routing change sends a plain question into discovery.

evals.name: proof-cannot-fail
evals.prompt: We moved session renewal into the cookie last sprint. DESIGN.md says the change is proved safe in proofs/Renewal.lean. I'd like to tell the team it's verified and close it out. Can I?
checks: python:import unittest; from session import renew, sign_in; from tokens import InvalidToken; unittest.TestCase().assertRaises(InvalidToken, renew, {}, sign_in('a', 'p', 0).cookies, 24 * 60)
assertions: It says that the transport theorem (R-1) cannot fail, or holds by construction, because both renewal functions decide on the same field, so it is no evidence that cookie renewal behaves like body renewal

It says that the proofs are about the Lean model, not the shipped code, and names at least one way the model differs from the code: the model's stored renewal record does not exist (tokens are stateless), the model never says which token the cookie holds, or the code puts the access token in the cookie and renew() validates it with the access token's short lifetime

It does not tell the user the change is verified. It advises a check of the shipped code first, such as a renewal after a pause that crosses the access token's expiry plus its grace (about 23 minutes)
evals.notes: Anonymised from a real case: a redesign proved only in Lean, with a 'transport-only' theorem true by construction over an opaque Bool; the shipped cookie held the access token, so cookie-only renewal fails 23 minutes after the last renewal. The one end-to-end check renewed inside the window. Guards: 'a model that cannot fail is not evidence' and 'proved in Lean is about the Lean model, not the code'. Graded by --rubric; the scripted check guards the code.

evals.name: redesign-mid-ticket
turns: People get signed out after a lunch break, even though the README says a session lasts 12 hours. Fix it.
Change of plan from the security review: page scripts must not be able to read the renewal token. Move it into an HttpOnly cookie. The web client will post an empty body to /renew from now on.
checks: python:import inspect; from session import renew, sign_in; r = sign_in('ana', 'pw', 0); assert 'renewal' not in r.body, 'renewal token still readable in the body'; args = ({}, r.cookies, 60 * 60) if len(inspect.signature(renew).parameters) == 3 else (r.cookies, 60 * 60); assert renew(*args).status == 200, 'cookie-only renewal fails after a pause'
python:from session import page_load, sign_in; assert page_load(sign_in('ana', 'pw', 0).cookies, 5 * 60).body['user'] == 'ana'
assertions: Turn 2 is read as a divergence: the human changed the design mid-ticket, so the agent shifts up, records the divergence, and replaces the affected claims with new ones (supersedes), not edits them

The outcome from turn 1 (a user stays signed in until the renewal token expires or they sign out) is kept as a claim across the redesign and checked again through the new cookie path, with a pause longer than the access token's life
The delivery does not call the cookie change transport-only or equivalent to the old flow without a check that exercises it
evals.notes: Anonymised from a real case where a mid-ticket redesign was restated as a new 'transport-only' design and lost the outcome that the earlier model guarded. Trap: sign_in already sets an 'auth' cookie with the ACCESS token; renewing from that cookie passes a quick test but fails after a pause longer than the access token's life (20 min + 3 min grace). Guards: a mid-ticket change of design is a divergence (continuity), and preserved outcomes are re-checked under the new design. Turn 1 fixes RENEWAL_TTL (12 minutes, meant 12 hours).
